{{Short description|Statistical concept}}
In [[statistics]], '''missing data''', or '''missing values''', occur when no [[data]] [[Value (mathematics)|value]] is stored for the [[Variable (mathematics)|variable]] in an [[unit of observation#Data point|observation]].  Missing data are a common occurrence and can have a significant effect on the conclusions that can be drawn from the data.

Missing data can occur because of nonresponse: no information is provided for one or more items or for a whole unit ("subject"). Some items are more likely to generate a nonresponse than others: for example items about private subjects such as income. [[Attrition (epidemiology)|Attrition]] is a type of missingness that can occur in longitudinal studies—for instance studying development where a measurement is repeated after a certain period of time. Missingness occurs when participants drop out before the test ends and one or more measurements are missing.

Data often are missing in research in [[economics]], [[sociology]], and [[political science]] because governments or private entities choose not to, or fail to, report critical statistics,<ref>{{cite journal | author = Messner SF | year = 1992 | title = Exploring the Consequences of Erratic Data Reporting for Cross-National Research on Homicide | journal = Journal of Quantitative Criminology | volume = 8 | issue = 2| pages = 155–173 | doi=10.1007/bf01066742| s2cid = 133325281 }}</ref> or because the information is not available. Sometimes missing values are caused by the researcher—for example, when data collection is done improperly or mistakes are made in data entry.<ref name="AM 2008">{{cite book|title=Advising on Research Methods: A Consultant's Companion|last2=Adèr|first2=Herman J.|last3=Mellenbergh|first3=Gideon J.|date=2008|publisher=Johannes van Kessel|isbn=978-90-79418-01-5|location=Huizen, Netherlands|pages=305–332|last1=Hand|first1=David J.}}</ref>

These forms of missingness take different types, with different impacts on the validity of conclusions from research: Missing completely at random, missing at random, and missing not at random.  Missing data can be handled similarly as [[censored data]].

==Types==
Understanding the reasons why data are missing is important for handling the remaining data correctly. If values are missing completely at random, the data sample is likely still representative of the population. But if the values are missing systematically, analysis may be biased.  For example, in a study of the relation between IQ and income, if participants with an above-average IQ tend to skip the question 'What is your salary?', analyses that do not take into account this missing at random (MAR pattern (see below)) may falsely fail to find a positive association between IQ and salary.  Because of these problems, methodologists routinely advise researchers to design studies to minimize the occurrence of missing values.<ref name="AM 2008" /> Graphical models can be used to describe the missing data mechanism in detail.<ref name="moh:13" /><ref name="kar:15">{{cite journal|last=Karvanen|first=Juha|year=2015|title=Study design in causal models|journal=Scandinavian Journal of Statistics|volume=42|issue=2|pages=361&ndash;377|doi=10.1111/sjos.12110|arxiv=1211.2958|s2cid=53642701}}</ref>

[[File:Missing not at random.png|thumb|The graph shows the probability distributions of the estimations of the expected intensity of depression in the population. The number of cases is 60. Let the true population be a standardised normal distribution and the non-response probability be a logistic function of the intensity of depression. The conclusion is: The more data is missing (MNAR), the more biased are the estimations. We underestimate the intensity of depression in the population.]]

===Missing completely at random===

Values in a data set are '''missing completely at random (MCAR)''' if the events that lead to any particular data-item being missing are independent both of observable variables and of unobservable parameters of interest, and occur entirely at random.<ref name="Polit">{{cite book |author=Polit DF Beck CT |title=Nursing Research: Generating and Assessing Evidence for Nursing Practice, 9th ed. |year=2012 |publisher=Wolters Klower Health, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins |location=Philadelphia, USA}}</ref> When data are MCAR, the analysis performed on the data is unbiased; however, data are rarely MCAR.

In the case of MCAR, the missingness of data is unrelated to any study variable: thus, the participants with completely observed data are in effect a random sample of all the participants assigned a particular intervention. With MCAR, the random assignment of treatments is assumed to be preserved, but that is usually an unrealistically strong assumption in practice.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://onbiostatistics.blogspot.com/2012/10/missingness-mechanism-mcar-mar-and-mnar.html |title=On Biostatistics and Clinical Trials |author=Deng |access-date=13 May 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160315011709/http://onbiostatistics.blogspot.com/2012/10/missingness-mechanism-mcar-mar-and-mnar.html |archive-date=15 March 2016 |date=2012-10-05 }}</ref>

===Missing at random===
'''Missing at random (MAR)''' occurs when the missingness is not random, but where missingness can be fully accounted for by variables where there is complete information.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://missingdata.lshtm.ac.uk/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=76%3Amissing-at-random-mar&catid=40%3Amissingness-mechanisms&Itemid=96 |title=Home |access-date=2015-08-01 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150910180057/http://missingdata.lshtm.ac.uk/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=76:missing-at-random-mar&catid=40:missingness-mechanisms&Itemid=96 |archive-date=2015-09-10 }}</ref> Since MAR is an assumption that is impossible to verify statistically, we must rely on its substantive reasonableness.<ref>{{citation  |last2=Rubin | first2= Donald B. | author2-link= Donald Rubin | last1=Little | first1= Roderick J. A. |title=Statistical Analysis with Missing Data |publisher= [[Wiley (publisher)|Wiley]] |year=2002 |edition=2nd | bibcode= 2002samd.book.....L }}.</ref> An example is that males are less likely to fill in a depression survey but this has nothing to do with their level of depression, after accounting for maleness. Depending on the analysis method, these data can still induce parameter bias in analyses due to the contingent emptiness of cells (male, very high depression may have zero entries). However, if the parameter is estimated with Full Information Maximum Likelihood, MAR will provide asymptotically unbiased estimates. {{Citation needed|date=June 2016}}

===Missing not at random===

'''Missing not at random (MNAR)''' (also known as nonignorable nonresponse) is data that is neither MAR nor MCAR (i.e. the value of the variable that's missing is related to the reason it's missing).<ref name=Polit /> To extend the previous example, this would occur if men failed to fill in a depression survey ''because'' of their level of depression.

Samuelson and Spirer (1992) discussed how missing and/or distorted data about demographics, law enforcement, and health could be indicators of patterns of human rights violations.  They gave several fairly well documented examples.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Samuelson |first1=Douglas A. |chapter=Chapter 3. Use of Incomplete and Distorted Data in Inference About Human Rights Violations |date=1992-12-31 |title=Human Rights and Statistics |pages=62–78 |publisher=University of Pennsylvania Press |last2=Spirer |first2=Herbert F.|doi=10.9783/9781512802863-006 |isbn=978-1-5128-0286-3 |chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Structured missingness ===
Missing data can also arise in subtle ways that are not well accounted for in classical theory. An increasingly encountered problem arises in which data may not be MAR but missing values exhibit an association or structure, either explicitly or implicitly. Such missingness has been described as 'structured missingness'.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Mitra |first1=Robin |last2=McGough |first2=Sarah F. |last3=Chakraborti |first3=Tapabrata |last4=Holmes |first4=Chris |last5=Copping |first5=Ryan |last6=Hagenbuch |first6=Niels |last7=Biedermann |first7=Stefanie |last8=Noonan |first8=Jack |last9=Lehmann |first9=Brieuc |last10=Shenvi |first10=Aditi |last11=Doan |first11=Xuan Vinh |last12=Leslie |first12=David |last13=Bianconi |first13=Ginestra |last14=Sanchez-Garcia |first14=Ruben |last15=Davies |first15=Alisha |date=2023-01-25 |title=Learning from data with structured missingness |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s42256-022-00596-z |journal=Nature Machine Intelligence |language=en |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=13–23 |doi=10.1038/s42256-022-00596-z |issn=2522-5839|arxiv=2304.01429 }}</ref>

Structured missingness commonly arises when combining information from multiple studies, each of which may vary in its design and measurement set and therefore only contain a subset of variables from the union of measurement modalities. In these situations, missing values may relate to the various sampling methodologies used to collect the data or reflect characteristics of the wider population of interest, and so may impart useful information. For instance, in a health context, structured missingness has been observed as a consequence of linking clinical, genomic and imaging data.<ref name=":0" />

The presence of structured missingness may be a hindrance to make effective use of data at scale, including through both classical statistical and current machine learning methods. For example, there might be bias inherent in the reasons why some data might be missing in patterns, which might have implications in predictive fairness for machine learning models. Furthermore, established methods for dealing with missing data, such as [[Imputation (statistics)|imputation]], do not usually take into account the structure of the missing data and so development of new formulations is needed to deal with structured missingness appropriately or effectively. Finally, characterising structured missingness within the classical framework of MCAR, MAR, and MNAR is a work in progress.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Jackson |first1=James |title=A Complete Characterisation of Structured Missingness |date=2023-07-05 |arxiv=2307.02650 |last2=Mitra |first2=Robin |last3=Hagenbuch |first3=Niels |last4=McGough |first4=Sarah |last5=Harbron |first5=Chris}}</ref>

=== Planned missingness ===
Missing data can also be a deliberate part of study design. Specifically, planned missingness is a research design strategy, employed in survey research, in which data are intentionally left uncollected from individual respondents (typically by administering randomly sampled subsets of items to each participant) to reduce burden while preserving the ability to estimate parameters for the full item set across the sample.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Charlene |last2=Yu |first2=Martin C. |date=October 2022 |title=Planned Missingness: How to and How Much? |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10944281211016534 |journal=Organizational Research Methods |language=en |volume=25 |issue=4 |pages=623–641 |doi=10.1177/10944281211016534 |issn=1094-4281|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Charlene |last2=Sackett |first2=Paul R. |title=Planned missingness: An underused but practical approach to reducing survey and test length |journal=Industrial and Organizational Psychology |date=March 2023 |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=129–142 |doi=10.1017/iop.2022.113}}</ref>

==Techniques of dealing with missing data==
Missing data reduces the representativeness of the sample and can therefore distort inferences about the population. Generally speaking, there are three main approaches to handle missing data: (1) ''Imputation''—where values are filled in the place of missing data, (2) ''omission''—where samples with invalid data are discarded from further analysis and (3) ''analysis''—by directly applying methods unaffected by the missing values. One systematic review addressing the prevention and handling of missing data for patient-centered outcomes research identified 10 standards as necessary for the prevention and handling of missing data. These include standards for study design, study conduct, analysis, and reporting.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Li|first1=Tianjing|last2=Hutfless|first2=Susan|last3=Scharfstein|first3=Daniel O.|last4=Daniels|first4=Michael J.|last5=Hogan|first5=Joseph W.|last6=Little|first6=Roderick J.A.|last7=Roy|first7=Jason A.|last8=Law|first8=Andrew H.|last9=Dickersin|first9=Kay|date=2014|title=Standards should be applied in the prevention and handling of missing data for patient-centered outcomes research: a systematic review and expert consensus|journal=Journal of Clinical Epidemiology|language=en|volume=67|issue=1|pages=15–32|doi=10.1016/j.jclinepi.2013.08.013|pmc=4631258|pmid=24262770}}</ref>

In some practical application, the experimenters can control the level of missingness, and prevent missing values before gathering the data. For example, in computer questionnaires, it is often not possible to skip a question. A question has to be answered, otherwise one cannot continue to the next. So missing values due to the participant are eliminated by this type of questionnaire, though this method may not be permitted by an ethics board overseeing the research. In survey research, it is common to make multiple efforts to contact each individual in the sample, often sending letters to attempt to persuade those who have decided not to participate to change their minds.<ref name="Stoop 2010">{{cite book |last1=Stoop |first1=I.|author1-link= Ineke Stoop |last2=Billiet |first2=J. |last3=Koch |first3=A. |last4=Fitzgerald |first4=R. |title=Reducing Survey Nonresponse: Lessons Learned from the European Social Survey |date=2010 |publisher=Wiley-Blackwell |location=Oxford |isbn=978-0-470-51669-0}}</ref>{{rp|161–187}} However, such techniques can either help or hurt in terms of reducing the negative inferential effects of missing data, because the kind of people who are willing to be persuaded to participate after initially refusing or not being home are likely to be significantly different from the kinds of people who will still refuse or remain unreachable after additional effort.<ref name="Stoop 2010" />{{rp|188–198}}

In situations where missing values are likely to occur, the researcher is often advised on planning to use methods of data analysis methods that are [[robust statistics|robust]] to missingness. An analysis is robust when we are confident that mild to moderate violations of the technique's key assumptions will produce little or no [[bias]], or distortion in the conclusions drawn about the population.

===Imputation===
{{Main|Imputation (statistics)}}
Some [[data analysis]] techniques are not robust to missingness, and require to "fill in", or [[Imputation (statistics)|impute]] the missing data. Rubin (1987) argued that repeating imputation even a few times (five or less) enormously improves the quality of estimation.<ref name="AM 2008"/> For many practical purposes, two or three imputations capture most of the relative efficiency that could be captured with a larger number of imputations.  However, a too-small number of imputations can lead to a substantial loss of [[statistical power]], and some scholars now recommend 20 to 100 or more.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Graham J.W. |author2=Olchowski A.E. |author3=Gilreath T.D. | year = 2007 | title = How Many Imputations Are Really Needed? Some Practical Clarifications of Multiple Imputation Theory | journal = Preventative Science | volume = 8 | issue = 3| pages = 208–213 | doi = 10.1007/s11121-007-0070-9 |pmid=17549635 |s2cid=24566076 }}</ref>  Any multiply-imputed data analysis must be repeated for each of the imputed data sets and, in some cases, the relevant statistics must be combined in a relatively complicated way.<ref name="AM 2008" /> Multiple imputation is not conducted in specific disciplines, as there is a lack of training or misconceptions about them.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=van Ginkel |first1=Joost R. |last2=Linting |first2=Marielle |last3=Rippe |first3=Ralph C. A. |last4=van der Voort |first4=Anja |date=2020-05-03 |title=Rebutting Existing Misconceptions About Multiple Imputation as a Method for Handling Missing Data |journal=Journal of Personality Assessment |volume=102 |issue=3 |pages=297–308 |doi=10.1080/00223891.2018.1530680 |issn=0022-3891 |pmid=30657714|s2cid=58580667 |hdl=1887/138825 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Methods such as listwise deletion have been used to impute data but it has been found to introduce additional bias.<ref>{{Cite book |last=van Buuren |first=S. |title=Flexible imputation of missing data |publisher=CRC Press |year=2018 |edition=2nd}}</ref> There is a beginner guide that provides a step-by-step instruction how to impute data.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Woods |first1=Adrienne D. |last2=Gerasimova |first2=Daria |last3=Van Dusen |first3=Ben |last4=Nissen |first4=Jayson |last5=Bainter |first5=Sierra |last6=Uzdavines |first6=Alex |last7=Davis-Kean |first7=Pamela E. |last8=Halvorson |first8=Max |last9=King |first9=Kevin M. |last10=Logan |first10=Jessica A. R. |last11=Xu |first11=Menglin |last12=Vasilev |first12=Martin R. |last13=Clay |first13=James M. |last14=Moreau |first14=David |last15=Joyal-Desmarais |first15=Keven |date=2023-02-23 |title=Best practices for addressing missing data through multiple imputation |journal=Infant and Child Development |volume=33 |article-number=e2407 |language=en |doi=10.1002/icd.2407 |issn=1522-7227|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The [[expectation-maximization algorithm]] is an approach in which values of the statistics which would be computed if a complete dataset were available are estimated (imputed), taking into account the pattern of missing data. In this approach, values for individual missing data-items are not usually imputed.

==== Interpolation ====
{{Main|Interpolation}}
In the mathematical field of numerical analysis, [[interpolation]] is a method of constructing new data points within the range of a discrete set of known data points.

In the comparison of two paired samples with missing data, a test statistic that uses all available data without the need for imputation is the partially overlapping samples [[t-test]].<ref name="POT">{{cite journal|last1=Derrick|first1=B|last2=Russ|first2=B|last3=Toher|first3=D|last4=White|first4=P|date=2017|title=Test Statistics for the Comparison of Means for Two Samples That Include Both Paired and Independent Observations|journal= Journal of Modern Applied Statistical Methods|volume=16|issue=1|pages=137–157|doi=10.22237/jmasm/1493597280|doi-access=free}}</ref> This is valid under normality and assuming MCAR

===Partial deletion===
Methods which involve reducing the data available to a dataset having no missing values include:
* [[Listwise deletion]]/casewise deletion
* Pairwise deletion

===Full analysis===
Methods which take full account of all information available, without the distortion resulting from using imputed values as if they were actually observed:
* Generative approaches:
**The [[expectation-maximization algorithm]]
** full information [[maximum likelihood]] estimation
*Discriminative approaches:
**Max-margin classification of data with absent features <ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chechik|first1=Gal|last2=Heitz|first2=Geremy|last3=Elidan|first3=Gal|last4=Abbeel|first4=Pieter|last5=Koller|first5=Daphne|date=2008-06-01|title=Max-margin Classification of incomplete data|url=http://papers.nips.cc/paper/3024-max-margin-classification-of-incomplete-data.pdf|journal=Neural Information Processing Systems|pages=233–240|author4-link=Pieter Abbeel}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chechik|first1=Gal|last2=Heitz|first2=Geremy|last3=Elidan|first3=Gal|last4=Abbeel|first4=Pieter|last5=Koller|first5=Daphne|date=2008-06-01|title=Max-margin Classification of Data with Absent Features|url=http://dl.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=1390681.1390682|journal=The Journal of Machine Learning Research|volume=9|pages=1–21|issn=1532-4435|author4-link=Pieter Abbeel}}</ref>

[[Partial identification]] methods may also be used.<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1146/annurev.economics.050708.143401| volume = 2| issue = 1| pages = 167–195| last = Tamer| first = Elie| title = Partial Identification in Econometrics| journal = [[Annual Review of Economics]]| date = 2010| url = http://scholar.harvard.edu/files/tamer/files/pie.pdf}}</ref>

==Model-based techniques==
Model based techniques, often using graphs, offer
additional tools for testing missing data types (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and for estimating parameters under missing data conditions. For example, a test for refuting MAR/MCAR reads as follows:

For any three variables ''X,Y'', and ''Z'' where ''Z'' is fully observed and ''X'' and ''Y'' partially observed, the data should satisfy:
<math>X \perp\!\!\!\perp R_y |(R_x,Z)</math>.

In words, the observed portion of ''X'' should be independent on the missingness status of ''Y,'' conditional on every value of ''Z''.
Failure to satisfy this condition indicates that the problem belongs to the MNAR category.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Mohan|first1=Karthika|last2=Pearl|first2=Judea|title=On the testability of models with missing data|journal=Proceedings of AISTAT-2014, Forthcoming|date=2014}}</ref>

(Remark:
These tests are necessary for variable-based MAR which is a slight variation of event-based MAR.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Darwiche|first1=Adnan|title=Modeling and Reasoning with Bayesian Networks|date=2009|publisher=Cambridge University Press}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Potthoff|first1=R.F.|last2=Tudor|first2=G.E.|last3=Pieper|first3=K.S.|last4=Hasselblad|first4=V.|title=Can one assess whether missing data are missing at random in medical studies?|journal=Statistical Methods in Medical Research|date=2006|volume=15|issue=3|pages=213–234|doi=10.1191/0962280206sm448oa|pmid=16768297|s2cid=12882831}}</ref><ref name="pearl:mohan2013-r417">{{cite tech report |last1=Pearl|first1=Judea|last2=Mohan|first2=Karthika|title=Recoverability and Testability of Missing data: Introduction and Summary of Results |institution=UCLA Computer Science Department, R-417 |year=2013 |url=http://ftp.cs.ucla.edu/pub/stat_ser/r417.pdf}}</ref>)

When data falls into MNAR category, techniques are available for consistently estimating parameters when certain conditions hold in the model.<ref name="moh:13">{{cite book|last1=Mohan|first1=Karthika|last2=Pearl|first2=Judea|last3=Tian|first3=Jin|chapter=Graphical Models for Inference with Missing Data |title=Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 26|date=2013|pages=1277–1285 |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/6mk2b174}}</ref>
For example, if ''Y'' explains the reason for missingness in ''X,'' and ''Y'' itself has missing values, the [[joint probability distribution]] of ''X'' and ''Y'' can still be estimated if the
missingness of ''Y'' is random.
The estimand in this case will be:
:<math>
\begin{align}
P(X,Y)& =P(X|Y) P(Y) \\
         & =P(X|Y,R_x=0,R_y=0) P(Y|R_y=0)
\end{align}
</math>
where <math>R_x=0</math> and <math>R_y=0</math> denote the observed portions of their respective variables.

Different model structures may yield different estimands and different procedures of estimation whenever consistent estimation is possible.  The preceding estimand calls for first
estimating <math>P(X|Y)</math> from complete data and multiplying it by <math>P(Y)</math> estimated from cases in which ''Y'' is observed  regardless of the status of ''X''. Moreover, in order to
obtain a consistent estimate it is crucial that the first term be <math>P(X|Y)</math> as opposed to <math>P(Y|X)</math>.

In many cases model based techniques permit the model structure to undergo refutation tests.<ref name="pearl:mohan2013-r417"/>
Any model which implies the independence between a partially observed variable ''X'' and the missingness indicator of another variable ''Y'' (i.e. <math>R_y</math>), conditional
on <math>R_x</math> can be submitted to  the following refutation test:
<math>X \perp\!\!\!\perp R_y | R_x =0</math>.

Finally, the estimands that emerge from these techniques are derived in closed form and do not require iterative procedures such as Expectation Maximization that
are susceptible to local optima.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Mohan|first1=K.|last2=Van den Broeck|first2=G.|last3=Choi|first3=A.|last4=Pearl|first4=J.|title=An Efficient Method for Bayesian Network Parameter Learning from Incomplete Data|journal=Presented at Causal Modeling and Machine Learning Workshop, ICML-2014|date=2014}}</ref>

A special class of problems appears when the probability of the missingness depends on time. For example, in the trauma databases the probability to lose data about the trauma outcome depends on the day after trauma. In these cases various non-stationary [[Markov chain]] models are applied.
<ref name="Mirkes2016">{{cite journal| last1 = Mirkes| first1 = E.M.| last2 = Coats| first2 = T.J.| last3 = Levesley| first3 = J.| last4 = Gorban| first4 = A.N.| title = Handling missing data in large healthcare dataset: A case study of unknown trauma outcomes| url = https://www.researchgate.net/publication/300400110| journal = Computers in Biology and Medicine| volume = 75| pages = 203–216| year = 2016| doi = 10.1016/j.compbiomed.2016.06.004| pmid = 27318570| url-status = live| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160805184827/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/300400110_Handling_missing_data_in_large_healthcare_dataset_A_case_study_of_unknown_trauma_outcomes| archive-date = 2016-08-05| arxiv = 1604.00627| bibcode = 2016arXiv160400627M| s2cid = 5874067}}</ref>
